title: Lung mass with hiccups, shoulder pain, dyspnea: phrenic nerve (C3-C5) compression
vignette: A 65-year-old man with a long history of smoking comes to the office due to a nonproductive cough over the last several months. He recently developed left shoulder pain, persistent hiccups, and dyspnea. His temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg, and pulse is 76/min. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds on the left side. Chest x-ray shows a large left lung mass. Compression of a nerve arising from which of the following locations is most likely causing this patient's recent symptoms?

clues.text: left shoulder pain, persistent hiccups, and dyspnea
clues.note: Shoulder pain (referred from C3-C4), persistent hiccups (diaphragmatic irritation), and dyspnea (diaphragm paralysis) all point to PHRENIC nerve involvement.
A lung tumor can compress/invade the phrenic nerve as it courses through the thorax, producing these symptoms.

whatMatters: The PHRENIC NERVE arises from C3-C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive') and innervates the diaphragm. A lung mass compressing it causes DYSPNEA (diaphragm paralysis), HICCUPS (diaphragmatic irritation), and referred SHOULDER PAIN (C3-C4 dermatomes). Answer C (C3-C5).
strategy: Match the symptom triad (shoulder pain + hiccups + dyspnea) to the phrenic nerve, then recall its origin: C3-C5. Reject other levels/structures: brainstem (cranial nerves/long tracts, not phrenic), C1-C3 (neck musculature; wouldn't explain hiccups/dyspnea), C5-C8 (brachial plexus - arm), and T1-T2 (lower brachial plexus/sympathetics - Horner/hand).

eliminations.label: Brainstem - cranial nerves/long tracts
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the origin of most cranial nerves and site of the respiratory center. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a peripheral lung mass compresses the phrenic nerve in the thorax, not the brainstem; brainstem lesions give cranial nerve/long-tract signs. ✅ Correct if: central (brainstem) pathology.

eliminations.label: C1-C3 - neck muscles, not diaphragm
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: upper cervical roots (C1 is largely motor; neck musculature). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they don't form the phrenic nerve or explain hiccups/dyspnea. ✅ Correct if: upper neck/cervical musculature.

eliminations.label: C5-C8 - brachial plexus (arm)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: roots contributing to the brachial plexus (upper limb). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a lung apex tumor invading C8-T1 causes arm/hand symptoms (Pancoast), not diaphragmatic paralysis/hiccups. ✅ Correct if: brachial plexopathy (shoulder/arm).

eliminations.label: T1-T2 - lower plexus/sympathetics
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: roots feeding the lower brachial plexus and sympathetic chain. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: involvement causes hand weakness or Horner syndrome (via sympathetic disruption), not phrenic symptoms. ✅ Correct if: Horner syndrome / T1 hand findings.

reasoning: Shoulder pain + persistent hiccups + dyspnea localize to the phrenic nerve/diaphragm
The phrenic nerve arises from the C3-C5 cervical roots
A left lung mass can compress the phrenic nerve in the thorax
mechanism: The PHRENIC NERVE arises from the C3-C5 cervical spinal segments ('C3, 4, 5 KEEP THE DIAPHRAGM ALIVE') and descends through the neck and thorax (anterior to the scalene/lung hilum) to provide the sole motor supply to the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm (and sensory fibers to the mediastinal pleura, pericardium, and central diaphragm). LUNG CANCERS spread locally and can compress or invade the phrenic nerve, causing: DYSPNEA and diaphragmatic PARALYSIS (with elevation of the affected hemidiaphragm and paradoxical upward motion on inspiration seen on fluoroscopy); persistent HICCUPS from diaphragmatic irritation; and REFERRED SHOULDER PAIN (the C3-C4 supraclavicular dermatomes overlap the diaphragm's afferents). Other intrathoracic tumor syndromes include Horner syndrome and brachial plexopathy (apical/Pancoast tumors invading the sympathetic chain and C8-T1), SVC syndrome (central tumors, especially small cell), hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), and dysphagia (esophageal compression). The correct nerve origin is therefore C3-C5.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > phrenic nerve: C3-C5; sole motor to diaphragm; irritation -> hiccups, referred shoulder pain (C3-C4), diaphragm paralysis/dyspnea; lung cancer local syndromes: phrenic (hiccups), recurrent laryngeal (hoarseness), Horner/brachial plexus (Pancoast), SVC.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Hiccups + shoulder pain + dyspnea from a lung mass = phrenic nerve (C3-C5).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on phrenic nerve, C3-C5, diaphragm paralysis, referred pain, or Pancoast/Horner syndrome? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: C5-C8/T1-T2 = brachial plexus/sympathetics (arm/Horner); C1-C3 = neck; brainstem = central.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: phrenic nerve = C3-C5; lung tumor compression -> hiccups, referred shoulder pain, diaphragm paralysis/dyspnea.

keywords.back: Hiccups, referred shoulder pain, dyspnea (diaphragm paralysis)

firstAid.detail: Path > phrenic, recurrent laryngeal, Pancoast, SVC.

memoryHook: C3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive; a lung tumor pinching that phrenic nerve gives hiccups, a shrugged-shoulder ache, and breathlessness.
